# 4. Decisions & Choices

You have followed tea from plant to cup, through the body, and out into history and ritual. Here is the question that hangs over the whole journey—especially for anyone who makes hard choices for a living:

**Does the cup change how we choose?**

Drinks do not flip a magic "smart switch." They can **nudge** how fast you answer, how much risk you take, how much you care about tomorrow, and how trusting you are in a first move. Psychologists talk about fast gut thinking versus slow careful thinking. Economists and psychologists use lab games (balloons, trust games, ultimatum offers) to measure those nudges. Real life still depends on stakes and setting—and a lab dose is not the same as your everyday mug.


Imagine a balloon on a computer screen. Each pump earns a little money and raises the chance of a pop that wipes the trial. How far do you push? Now imagine the same task after alcohol, or after a matched theanine-caffeine drink, or after a washout weekend with no coffee. That is the flavor of evidence in this chapter: small, timed, artificial—and still useful if you refuse to overclaim.

Treat study findings as **careful hints**, not life rules. The packs show patterns for tea, high-caffeine coffee stress, and alcohol—in isolated lab conditions. Stake size, habit, and social setting all matter outside the lab. The owner of this site is an economist; we still do **not** invent economic theories here. We only retell what the packs and named papers already support. Tap a footnote marker to jump to the source, then tap the caret to jump back—Wikipedia-style. Hover often shows a popup too. Collapsed "More detail…" boxes hold denser task tables and protocol checklists.

::: {.callout-tip title="Words to know on this journey"}
- **System 1 / System 2** — fast automatic thinking vs slow careful thinking (dual-process idea).
- **Loss aversion** — feeling losses more strongly than equal gains (summarized with a number λ; if λ > 1, losses weigh more).
- **Present bias** — preferring a smaller reward *now* over a larger one later.
- **Trust Game / Ultimatum / Prisoner's Dilemma** — classic lab games about sending money, splitting offers, and cooperating.
- **BART** — Balloon Analogue Risk Task; how far people pump a virtual balloon.
- **Washout** — a period before a study when people avoid caffeine, alcohol, etc., so the test is cleaner.
:::

## Fast blurts and careful checks

Psychologists often talk about two modes (Kahneman's dual-process framing, building on earlier work with Tversky):

- **System 1** — fast, automatic, low effort.  
- **System 2** — slow, careful, effortful [^1].

Tea patterns in these packs are described as helping keep impulsive reactions in check, with L-theanine + caffeine synergy linked with longer careful focus [^2]. Coffee under stress can push rapid shortcuts; it may help simple arithmetic but can suffer on complex reflective tasks (Rogers et al., 2013; pack). Alcohol makes System 1 dominant and careful control drops sharply—the classic "alcohol myopia" idea that intoxication narrows attention to the most immediate cues [^3].

System 1 is blurting an answer in a quiz show. System 2 is checking your work on a hard homework problem. Caffeine can speed the blurting; under time pressure or anxiety it can hurt the careful check. L-theanine + caffeine is studied for sustained attention—not for deleting every bias.

| Metric | System 1 | System 2 | Source frame |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Speed / effort | Fast, low metabolic cost | Slow, costly | Kahneman (2011) [^1] |
| Tea pattern in these packs | Helps keep impulsive reactions in check | L-theanine + caffeine synergy linked with longer careful focus | Owen et al. (2008) [^2] |
| Coffee pattern | Under stress, can push rapid shortcuts | May help simple arithmetic; can suffer on complex reflective tasks | Pack / Rogers line |
| Alcohol pattern | Becomes dominant | Careful control drops sharply | Steele & Josephs (1990) [^3] |

Study snapshots:

| Task | Condition | Finding | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Attention switching / memory distractibility | 100 mg L-theanine + 50 mg caffeine | Faster and more accurate switching at 60 min; less distractibility vs placebo | Owen et al. (2008) [^2] |
| Rapid Visual Information Processing | L-theanine + caffeine designs (Haskell line; pack) | Hits up; false alarms down in pack narrative | Haskell et al. (2008; pack) |
| Visuospatial attention + alpha EEG | 100 mg L-theanine + 50 mg caffeine | Higher hit rate and d´; lower tonic alpha read as engaged attention | Kelly et al. (2008) [^4] |
| Stroop interference | 200 mg L-theanine (pack) | Interference cost down about **28 ms** | Higashiyama et al. (2011; pack) |
| Cognitive Reflection Test | 200 mg caffeine vs placebo (pack) | Impulsive errors up about **14%** in one cited design | Brunyé et al. (2012; pack) |

Dual-process work treats this as a **spectrum of effort**, not a binary drink switch. Do not read the table as "coffee = dumb, tea = wise."

People love a neat slogan: "Coffee = System 1, tea = System 2." Too neat. Caffeine speeds basic responding; under time pressure or anxiety it can hurt hard reflective tasks. L-theanine + caffeine helps sustained attention, but bias reduction (anchoring, framing) still depends on the task and the person [^1][^2].

Dual-process work treats this as a **spectrum of effort**, not a binary drink switch.[^1] Alcohol makes System 1 dominant via alcohol myopia—attention narrows to the most immediate cues.[^3] Do not read any table as "coffee = dumb, tea = wise."

Chapter 2's L-theanine story connects here: by softening excess glutamate signaling, L-theanine is linked with better sustained attention on hard switching tasks—fewer false alarms on rapid attention tests in the packs. (See [Linkages](../linkages.qmd).)

Speed of thinking is one axis. Appetite for risk—and patience for tomorrow—is another.

## Losses that sting, tomorrows that fade

Two plain ideas shape a lot of choice research. Neither was invented for this website; both come from the prospect-theory and intertemporal-choice literatures that economists and psychologists already use.

**Loss aversion:** most people feel losses more strongly than equal gains. Researchers summarize that with a number λ; if λ > 1, losses weigh more [^5].

**Present bias:** people often prefer a smaller reward *now* over a larger one later. Strong present bias means "tomorrow counts for less." Alcohol research often describes a related narrowing: when intoxicated, people overweight what is immediate and underweight delayed costs [^3][^6].

How the packs describe drink states (qualitative, not a prescription):

| State | Loss sensitivity (λ idea) | Waiting for future rewards |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tea (described pattern) | Often stays in a balanced range (about **1.8–2.5** in the narrative framing) | More patience; present bias closer to stable |
| High-caffeine / high-cortisol coffee pattern | Can soften loss aversion → more aggressive risk seeking under stress | Mixed; depends on context |
| Alcohol | Loss sensitivity can collapse ("alcohol myopia") | Strong present bias; future costs fade |

Loss aversion in everyday clothes: losing $10 often stings more than finding $10 feels good. Present bias: "one cookie now" beats "two cookies tomorrow" for many people—especially when alcohol makes tomorrow fade.

Lab snapshots (isolated doses, not "your mug at work"):

| Task | Condition | Finding | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Balloon risk task (BART) | Alcohol ~0.08% BrAC (pack narrative of Lejuez designs) | Mean adjusted pumps higher than placebo | Lejuez et al. (2002) [^7] |
| Delay discounting | Alcohol ~0.06% BAC (pack) | Discount parameter *k* rises (future rewards worth less) | Reynolds et al. (2006; pack) |
| Loss aversion λ | 200 mg caffeine in trading simulation (pack) | λ **2.15 → 1.62** | Rogers et al. (2013; pack) |
| Alcohol + gambling paradigms | Intoxication | Riskier play consistent with alcohol myopia | George et al. (2005) [^6] |

Full Prospect Theory and hyperbolic-discounting equations are skipped here; the idea is the same in words. Kahneman and Tversky's original prospect-theory paper and later cumulative updates are the formal home for λ [^5]. See the Bibliography for those papers if you want the math.

Pure caffeine or ethanol in the lab can shift discounting or loss aversion. Jumping from that to "one green tea makes you a patient investor" overstates the evidence.

That slogan is popular. The packs push back: stake size, income, habit, and social setting all confound real choices. And remember Chapter 2's stress thread—when cortisol rises under pressure, softer loss aversion and riskier choices can show up together. Field work on traders even links endogenous steroids with risk-taking on real floors—another reminder that chemistry and choices meet under pressure, without turning tea into a trading system [^8].

Alcohol's boost of inhibitory signaling (Chapter 2) is linked with strong present bias—future costs weigh less. That is one reason the packs discuss alcohol beside "tomorrow counts for less," not only beside "feeling drunk."

| --- | --- | --- |

:::


Risk and patience are often measured alone. Trust and fairness need someone else in the room.

## Games of trust, fairness, and cooperation

These are classic lab games. "Nash" here just means the cold, self-interested prediction—not what people always do.

The **Ultimatum Game** asks one player to offer a split of a pot; the other can accept or reject (rejection zeros both payoffs). Cold theory says accept any positive crumb; real people often reject unfair splits [^9]. The **Trust Game** lets a first mover send money that grows; a second mover decides how much to return [^10]. The **Prisoner's Dilemma** (and its repeated cousins) asks whether to cooperate or defect when mutual cooperation beats mutual defection but temptation to defect is real [^11].

| Game | Cold prediction | Tea / warmth pattern in packs | Alcohol pattern in packs | Anchors |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ultimatum | Tiny offers; accept anything above zero | Offers nearer fair **40%–50%** splits | More rejection of unfair offers (≤ about 30%) | Güth et al. (1982); Morewedge et al. (2014) [^9][^12] |
| Prisoner's Dilemma | Both defect | More mutual cooperation | Volatile defection or sloppy play | Axelrod (1984) [^11] |
| Trust Game | Send nothing; return nothing | Higher first sends and more reciprocity | High sends with higher betrayal risk | Berg et al. (1995) [^10] |

Ultimatum: someone offers you a split of $10; if you reject, both get nothing. Cold theory says accept $1; many people reject unfair splits. Trust Game: you send money that grows; the other person decides how much to return. Opening trust is not the same as forever trust.

Snapshots:

| Game | Result | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ultimatum, alcohol ~0.06% BAC (N = 92) | Unfair-offer (≤20%) rejection **82.4%** vs **58.1%** placebo | Morewedge et al. (2014) [^12] |
| Trust Game / fairness, warm ~60°C mug | First-mover investment about **+24.8%** (pack narrative) | Kang et al. (2011) [^13] |
| Iterated Dilemma, warm drink (pack) | Mutual cooperation rounds 1–10: **62.5%** vs **47.2%** control | Inagaki & Eisenberger (2013; pack) [^14] |

Warmth and ritual can lift **opening** trust (about **+15% to +25%** in cited work). If the other side defects in later rounds, cooperation often collapses. Incentives still dominate over a long game—Axelrod's tournaments already taught that cooperation needs structure, not only good vibes [^11].

People sometimes hope: "Serve tea and the negotiation becomes win–win forever." Opening trust is real in cited work; forever cooperation is not. Ritual can also blunt the brain's error-alarm and lower anxiety (Chapter 3)—discussed in the packs alongside fewer hyper-aggressive rejections of unfair offers. Calmer bodies can mean less hair-trigger bargaining—not automatic fairness forever. And remember Chapter 3's replication caution: warmth effects on generosity are smaller and less reliable than early headlines suggested [^15].

| Game | Cold prediction | Tea / warmth pattern in packs | Alcohol pattern in packs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ultimatum | Tiny offers; accept anything above zero | Offers nearer fair **40%–50%** splits | More rejection of unfair offers (≤ ~30%) |
| Prisoner's Dilemma | Both defect | More mutual cooperation | Volatile defection or sloppy play |
| Trust Game | Send nothing; return nothing | Higher first sends and more reciprocity | High sends with higher betrayal risk |

Anchors: Güth et al. (1982) Ultimatum;[^9] Berg, Dickhaut & McCabe (1995) Trust Game;[^10] Axelrod (1984) cooperation structure.[^11]

## How careful studies are usually built

If you read a headline—"tea improves decisions!"—ask how the trial was built. Good trials try to separate the drug effect from expectation, temperature, and bitter taste.

Common standards in the packs:

- **Exclude** people with major sleep or heart disease, or very high daily caffeine (over about **400 mg/day**).  
- **Washout:** no coffee, tea, energy drinks, chocolate, or alcohol for at least **48 hours** (sometimes **72** for heavy users).  
- **Same cup experience:** **250 mL**, opaque insulated mug, about **60°C ± 2°C**, bitterness matched (e.g. tiny quinine in placebo).  
- **Timing:** start cognitive tests about **+40 minutes** after drinking—near typical peak timing for oral L-theanine (**35–50 min**) and caffeine (**30–60 min**).  
- **Tasks:** tools such as the Balloon Analogue Risk Task (BART) and Iowa Gambling Task (IGT) [^7][^16].  

Example active dose used in matched designs: **200 mg L-theanine + 100 mg caffeine** vs sensory-matched placebo [^17].

If one group gets hot, bitter, fragrant tea and the other gets plain lukewarm water, you may be measuring "this feels like tea" as much as chemistry. That is why packs stress opaque mugs, matched bitterness, and washout days. Holding temperature constant also matters because Chapter 3 showed that mere warmth can nudge social judgments—so a decision study that forgets mug temperature may mix pharmacology with thermal priming [^13][^14].

Decaf tea is **not** a perfect placebo: it still has trace caffeine (about **2–5 mg**) and leftover polyphenols. Matching astringency and umami without changing smell or look is hard. Without opaque, taste-matched delivery, studies may measure expectation as much as pharmacology.

The Iowa Gambling Task—originally used to study how people learn from wins and losses after prefrontal injury—is one more tool in the pack's "feedback learning" kit [^16]. BART measures how far people push a risky balloon before it pops [^7]. Neither task is "your career in a cup." Both are controlled ways to watch risk and learning under a drink.

Notice how the study clock matches Chapter 1 and Chapter 2: tests at about **+40 minutes** sit near the L-theanine and caffeine peaks you already met. The kitchen timing and the lab timing are the same story told twice.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: washout, matched mugs, and why decaf is not a perfect placebo"}

## What an economist's caution sounds like here

This site's owner is an economist. That is a reason for **humility**, not for inventing a private theory of tea-and-markets.

Prospect theory, present bias, trust games, and ultimatum bargaining already exist as shared tools [^5][^9][^10]. The packs use those tools to describe how *drink states* look in lab snapshots. They do not license claims like "tea makes you a rational investor" or "coffee ruins negotiations." Stake size, wealth, culture, sleep, and the other player's reputation usually dominate any beverage nudge.

So the economist-friendly reading of this chapter is:

- Treat λ, discount rates, and trust sends as **measured shifts under controlled doses**, not personality transplants.  
- Prefer studies that wash out caffeine, match sensory cues, and time the task to known peaks [^17].  
- Remember that alcohol myopia and fairness punishment can both be true in the same intoxicated Ultimatum session—people may reject unfairness more, not less [^3][^12].  
- Keep Chapter 3's warmth replication failure in view when someone sells "serve tea, win the deal" [^15].

Interesting? Yes. Fact-based? Only as far as the citations go. That is the deal.

You began with steam over leaves. You met two plants, a processing fork, a brew, and three compounds. You followed those compounds into alertness, calm, stress, and body signals. You zoomed out to silver and empire, monasteries and tea rooms, warm hands and ritual breaks. You ended in lab games that measure nudges—not magic switches—and in protocols that try to keep expectation honest.

- Alcohol myopia and fairness punishment can both be true in the same intoxicated Ultimatum session—people may reject unfairness *more*, not less.[^3][^12]
- Keep Chapter 3's warmth replication failure in view for "serve tea, win the deal" claims.[^15]
